objectives: Test a completed operation history against a register specification.
Distinguish real-time order from per-client program order.
Construct a sequentially consistent history that is not linearizable.
Separate consistency of individual operations from transaction isolation and read-modify-write atomicity.
retrieval: L071: can a timeout place a definite commit point in a history?
L038: why does transaction terminology need a stated isolation contract?
L066: what user behavior can replication lag expose?

sections.title: Start with the object before naming the guarantee
sections.markdown:
Our object is a register x, initially 0. write(v) replaces its value and returns success. read() returns the value of the latest preceding write in the chosen legal sequential order, or 0 if none precedes it. This specification is tiny enough to check by hand. A queue, set, compare-and-swap register, and multi-object transaction each require different legal behavior.

For each operation record client, invocation, response, argument, and result. Draw an interval from invocation to response. Use a trusted harness order for the exercise; production machine timestamps may be skewed. The ordering question is whether the observed operations can be arranged into a legal sequential execution under the required constraints. Do not start by guessing whether the implementation is “strong.”

Use 5 minutes retrieval, 20 history reasoning, 10 diagram walkthrough, 10 exercise, and 10 questions/cards. No consensus algorithm is needed yet; this lesson defines what one would need to provide.

sections.title: Linearizability preserves non-overlapping real-time order
sections.markdown:
Linearizability treats each operation as if it took effect at one instant inside its own invocation–response interval. The resulting sequential execution must satisfy the object specification. If operation A finishes before B begins, A must precede B. If they overlap, either order may be legal depending on the observed results. “Instantaneous” describes the external explanation, not the absence of internal network work.

History H1: Alice writes 1 during [1,4]; Bob reads during [2,3] and returns 0. This can be linearizable: place Bob’s read before Alice’s write because their intervals overlap. Alice’s write could take effect near time 3.5. Bob is not necessarily entitled to see a write that was still in progress throughout his read.

History H2: Alice writes 1 during [1,2]; Bob reads during [3,4] and returns 0. With no intervening write, this is not linearizable. Alice’s completed write must precede Bob’s invocation, and the register specification then demands 1. A response from a lagging replica explains how the history happened; it does not make the contract satisfied.

sections.title: Sequential consistency drops cross-client real-time constraints
sections.markdown:
Sequential consistency requires one legal sequential execution preserving each client’s program order. It need not preserve the wall-time order between different clients. H2 is sequentially consistent if Alice and Bob each perform only that one operation: order Bob’s read before Alice’s write in the explanation. That explanation contradicts real time but not either client’s local sequence.

Now H3 uses one client: Alice writes 1 successfully, then Alice reads 0, with no other writes. Per-client order forces the write before the read, so even sequential consistency fails. Asking “whose operation follows whose?” is essential. A stale result from another client and a stale result in the writer’s own program can differ in which guarantees they violate.

For a stronger test, let Alice execute write(x,1) then read(y)→0; Bob execute write(y,1) then read(x)→0, initially both zero. The first read requires Alice’s read before Bob’s write, and the second requires Bob’s read before Alice’s write. Combined with both program orders, these form a cycle. There is no single legal sequential order. This is an original two-register exercise; checking each register independently is insufficient to establish sequential consistency of the combined program.

sections.title: Work a history instead of using a slogan
sections.markdown:
Consider write(1) [1,5], read→1 [2,3], read→0 [6,7]. The first read can observe the overlapping write, but the final read cannot return 0: the write completed before it began. One allowed explanation for the prefix does not excuse the later violation.

Completed operations simplify the exercises. A real trace may contain an invocation without a response. A checker needs a stated treatment for those pending operations; an uncertain write may have taken effect. Deleting every timed-out operation from a trace can falsely accuse or falsely clear an implementation. The optional small checker in labs/consistency handles completed well-formed histories only and reports that boundary explicitly.

Linearizable read and write operations do not make a client-side increment atomic. Alice reads 0, Bob reads 0, Alice writes 1, Bob writes 1 is a perfectly legal linearizable register history. It loses an intended increment because the application required an atomic read-modify-write operation. Use an appropriate conditional or atomic increment contract, or a transaction whose actual guarantees enforce the invariant.

sections.title: State the scope and what evidence establishes
sections.markdown:
Serializability asks whether transactions have an equivalent serial execution; by itself it does not impose the same real-time constraint as strict serializability. Linearizability usually describes operations on concurrent objects. Do not use “ACID consistent,” “serializable,” and “linearizable” as interchangeable marketing words. State the unit: one key operation, a transaction over several keys, or a whole application workflow.

A leader label also does not prove linearizability. A stale follower read, a resumed old leader, or an acknowledged write lost on failover can invalidate the promised histories. Conversely, a correct protocol can hide substantial internal replication work behind a legal operation interval. The contract is about allowed observations, so verification must include invocation and response events plus relevant failure cases.

When explaining a design, say “a read begun after successful write completion must return that value or a later legal overwrite.” This is more assessable than “reads are up to date.” A finite passing test demonstrates the tested histories; it is not a proof over every schedule and failure. A single valid counterexample, however, disproves the claimed universal guarantee.

Sequential order B-read then A-write is legal
diagrams.caption: The final note assumes each client performs only its one shown operation and there are no other writes. Sequential consistency can reorder these different-client operations across real time.
steps: Real time forces write before read for linearizability.
The returned 0 then violates the register specification.
Removing cross-client real-time order permits the reversed sequential explanation.

exercise.prompt: For an initially-zero register classify three completed histories: (A) P writes1 [1,4], Q reads0 [2,3]; (B) P writes1 [1,2], Q reads0 [3,4]; (C) P writes1 [1,2], then P reads0 [3,4]. For each, state linearizable and sequentially consistent yes/no, and supply an ordering or contradiction. Assume no other operations.
rubric: A allows overlapping read before write.
B rejects real-time order but permits different-client reversal.
C preserves P’s program order and rejects both.
Uses the register specification rather than replica labels.
exercise.solution: A: yes/yes; order Q-read0 then P-write1, with the write linearization point after the read. B: no/yes; real time requires P-write1 before Q-read, but sequential consistency may order Q-read0 before P-write1. C: no/no; P’s own write precedes P’s read in both required orders, so return0 is illegal without a later overwrite.

questions.prompt: A read overlapping write1 returns the previous value. Must linearizability be violated?
questions.explanation: The overlapping read can precede the write’s linearization point.

questions.prompt: Which extra ordering does linearizability preserve beyond a legal sequential explanation?
questions.explanation: Response-before-invocation requires the earlier operation first.

questions.prompt: Why can two linearizable reads and two linearizable writes lose an increment?
questions.answer: Each operation is atomic but the combined read-modify-write sequence is not; both clients can read0 and later write1.
questions.explanation: Choose the correct atomic operation or transaction boundary.

questions.prompt: Why is a timed-out write dangerous to omit from a checker?
questions.answer: It may have taken effect even though its response was not observed, affecting the legal explanation of subsequent reads.
questions.explanation: Pending-operation semantics must be part of the checker’s model.

questions.prompt: Does a finite passing history test prove all executions linearizable?
questions.answer: No. It verifies only the modeled observed histories; one counterexample can refute the guarantee, but finite success does not prove all schedules.

flashcards.back: An explanatory instant within an operation’s invocation–response interval.
May be ordered either way if the resulting object behavior is legal.
Each client’s program order within one legal sequential execution.
Separate read and write do not provide it.

flashcards.front: How to disprove a history claim?
flashcards.back: Show no allowed ordering satisfies the object specification.

mentalModel: A consistency guarantee is a rule for which sequential stories can explain observed operation intervals.

sources.title: Herlihy and Wing — Linearizability: A Correctness Condition for Concurrent Objects (1990)
